text:
To understand how a refrigerator maintains the cold temperature of our food, we must first understand that it is not a simple box of ice. Instead, it is a closed thermodynamic cycle, a carefully engineered system of heat transfer and pressure. The magic of a refrigerator lies in the continuous movement of refrigerant gas, which acts as the working fluid. This process relies on four main components: the compressor, condenser, expansion valve, and evaporator. By following the step-by-step flow of this cycle, we can appreciate the science behind our daily convenience.

The process begins with the compressor. This is the heart of the refrigeration system. When you turn on the refrigerator, the compressor draws in low-pressure refrigerant gas and forces it through a series of valves and pipes. The compressor does more work than the refrigerator does; it is the engine that powers the entire cycle. As the refrigerant is compressed, its pressure and temperature rise significantly. This high-pressure, high-temperature gas is now ready to be cooled down. The compressor then releases this hot gas into the condenser coils, which are typically located on the back or bottom of the refrigerator.
